readingInstruction: Read James 1:1-27. James writes to Jewish Christians scattered abroad, and the letter reads like a collection of wisdom sayings. Notice how trials, temptation, and the word of God are tied together, and how often James moves from hearing to doing.
settingTheScene: The author is James, the brother of Jesus, who became the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15; Galatians 1:19). He did not believe in Jesus during the earthly ministry (John 7:5), but the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7). This may be the earliest New Testament letter, written to Jewish believers scattered by persecution. It reads like the Sermon on the Mount applied to daily life. James begins by calling himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, a humble title for the Lord’s own brother.
observation: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds” (v. 2).
“For you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness” (v. 3).
“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (v. 5).
“Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life” (v. 12).
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire” (v. 14).
“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (v. 17).
“But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (v. 22).
“Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world” (v. 27).
interpretation:
James opens with a surprising command: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds.” He does not say to enjoy suffering but to consider it joy, because “the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.” Trials are the gym where faith grows strong. And when we lack wisdom to understand them, we are to ask God, who “gives generously to all without reproach.” God does not scold us for asking. But we must ask in faith, with no doubting, for the double-minded person is “like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.” He is unstable in all his ways.

The poor brother is told to boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because the rich will pass away like a flower in the grass. The verdict is given in verse 12: “Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.” The reward is life itself.

Then James separates trials from temptation. A trial tests us, and God uses it for good. But temptation is something else, and God never tempts anyone. “But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.” James traces the path with vivid pictures: desire is the bait, sin is the offspring, and death is the end. We cannot blame God or circumstances. On the contrary, “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change.” The Father gives only good, and he does not change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.

The rest of the chapter is about the word. “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.” We are to put away filthiness and “receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.” But the word must be obeyed: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.” The one who hears and does not do is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror and goes away, immediately forgetting what he was like. But the one who looks into “the perfect law, the law of liberty,” and perseveres, “being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.” The chapter ends with three tests of real religion: a controlled tongue, care for orphans and widows, and keeping oneself unstained from the world.
connection: Matthew 5:10-12 and Romans 5:3-5 also connect suffering to joy and hope. 1 Peter 1:6-7 speaks of faith tested by fire. 1 Kings 3:5-14 shows Solomon asking God for wisdom. Proverbs 2:1-6 says the LORD gives wisdom. Matthew 7:7-11 teaches us to ask a generous Father. Matthew 7:24-27 speaks of hearing and doing. Revelation 2:10 promises the crown of life. Deuteronomy 10:18 and Isaiah 1:17 command care for orphans and widows. Luke 8:21 says Jesus’ family are those who hear and do the word.
application:
Think of a trial you are in now. Say out loud: God is using this to produce steadfastness. Ask him for wisdom for it, and believe he gives generously.

Look at the path in verses 14 and 15. What desire is luring you? Name it, and flee it before it grows.

Pick one thing you read in the Bible this week and do it today.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for every good gift from him.
Ask him to teach you to count trials as joy, and ask for wisdom.
Ask him to make you a doer of the word.
